new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in a sesquisyllable the final syllable (the main syllable) is stressed and the preceding presyllable is reduced and unstressed. Stress is therefore predictable and word-final; nothing suggests contrastive stress. This is the general Chamic pattern (Thurgood 1996: 'all have developed final stress... Roglai... essentially unchanged'; Thurgood 1998: iambic PC stress), which Brunelle et al. apply to the Ma Nới Southern Raglai material they recorded rather than describe independently.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; register (not stress) is the contrast studied. Southern Raglai has lost onset voicing in plain and aspirated stops and developed a register contrast on the following vowel (Tạ 2009 cited).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated citation forms in a controlled wordlist recorded in a carrier context). The stress sentence is a family-level (Austroasiatic/Chamic) characterisation cited from Butler 2014 and Thomas 1992, not a Southern Raglai-specific finding; no Southern Roglai grammar or phonology sketch exists in Glottolog, and no source with a stress section was found.
new_statements.identity_note: Brunelle et al. 2022/2025 describe the Southern Raglai of Ma Nới commune (Ninh Sơn district, Ninh Thuận), which they treat as one dialect of Southern Raglai (sout3010, ISO rgs); they note the Rai dialect of Bình Thuận (a Glottolog alt-name of sout3010) is unexplored and that Cát Gia Raglai (cacg1235, ISO roc; Lee 1998) may or may not be a Southern Raglai subdialect. Lee 1998 explicitly excludes Cat Gia from Southern Roglai. Thurgood 1996's 'Roglai' is undifferentiated by dialect.

sources.note: Instrumental study of onset voicing/register in Northern Raglai (Phước Đại, Bác Ái) and Southern Raglai (Ma Nới commune, Ninh Sơn district, Ninh Thuận). Section 1.2 states, as a Chamic/Austroasiatic generalisation while introducing the two Raglai dialects: words are sesquisyllables 'whose final stressed syllable, the main syllable, is preceded by a reduced unstressed syllable, the presyllable'; section 2.2 builds the 60-word Southern Raglai list from monosyllables and 'sesquisyllables with open main syllables'. sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham. 1996. Language contact and the directionality of internal drift: the development of tones and registers in Chamic. Language 72(1): 1-31 (author preprint 'Chamic contact', 44 pp., own pagination).
sources.note: Abstract (preprint p. 2): the Chamic languages 'in contact with the Mon-Khmer languages, all have developed final stress with consequent phonotactic restructuring. Since then, some languages have remained essentially unchanged (Roglai, Rade, and Jarai)'; p. 6 repeats that Roglai 'remained largely unchanged' after PC. Comparative-historical; 'Roglai' undifferentiated by dialect.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page sout3010 (read 2026-09-17); Wikipedia 'Roglai language' (en) and 'Tiếng Ra Glai' (vi).
sources.note: Glottolog lists no descriptive reference for sout3010 at all (only Brunelle 2024 for subclassification, Campbell et al. 2022, Bradley 2007). Wikipedia en/vi: consonant/vowel charts, four dialects per Cobbey 1977 (Northern, Du Long, Southern, Cac Gia); nothing on stress; vi page cites Ninh Thuận Dept of Education 2018 'Tài liệu bồi dưỡng tiếng Raglai' (not located online).

sources.citation: Đinh Lư Giang, Marc Brunelle & Tạ Thành Tấn. 2025. Relating production and perception in two Raglai dialects at different stages of registrogenesis. Phonetica. DOI 10.1515/phon-2024-0032 (PMC11808351).
sources.note: Same two field sites (Ma Nới = Southern Raglai). Register production/perception only; full text contains no statement on stress, presyllables or main syllables.

sources.citation: Norquest, Peter. 2005. Word structure in Chamic: prosodic alignment versus segmental faithfulness. In Grant & Sidwell (eds), Chamic and Beyond (Pacific Linguistics 569), 147-188. DOI 10.15144/PL-569.147.
sources.note: Diachronic: PC shifted main stress to the word-final syllable under Mon-Khmer contact; Northern Roglai 'continued the prosodic structure of PC relatively unchanged'. Southern Roglai not treated.

sources.citation: Lee, Ernest W. 1998. The contribution of Cat Gia Roglai to Chamic. In David Thomas (ed.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 15: Further Chamic Studies (Pacific Linguistics A-89), 31-54. DOI 10.15144/PL-A89.31.
sources.note: Historical phonology of Cat Gia Roglai (a separate variety, cacg1235/roc, which Lee explicitly does not count as Southern Roglai, p. 31). Southern Roglai appears only in passing comparisons (e.g. some Southern Roglai dialects keep final nasals, p. 41ff; a Southern Roglai form for 'corn'). Uses 'pretonic'/'tonic syllable' but states no stress rule for any variety.

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham. 1998. Austronesian and Mon-Khmer components in the Proto Chamic vowel system. In Further Chamic Studies (PL A-89), 61-90. DOI 10.15144/PL-A89.61.
sources.note: p. 61: Proto-Chamic 'adopted the main-syllable stress of the neighbouring MK languages... an unstressed initial syllable followed by a stressed main syllable. This iambic PC stress pattern...'. Proto-language level only; Southern Roglai not described.
